paper_metadata.title: Quantum Financial Modeling on Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum Hardware: Random Walks using Approximate Quantum Counting

summary: The paper studies gate-based quantum approximate counting circuits for finance, comparing a 6-qubit binary counter and an 8-qubit arc counter / arc walk / random-jump family on ideal simulation, noisy simulation, and an 11-qubit trapped-ion QPU. Key reported numbers include the binary counter collapsing to about 31-34 average position after 10 steps under noise/QPU, while the arc counter remains much closer to the ideal trend (e.g. 17.836 ideal vs 18.459 noisy vs 19.666 QPU at step 10), and the arc walk / random-jump circuits produce broader heavy-tailed distributions but no demonstrated practical quantum advantage.

experiments.description: Binary counter and arc counter circuits run on ideal simulation, noisy simulation, and an 11-qubit trapped-ion QPU to compare how accurately they track monotonically increasing position over 0-10 steps.

algorithm.variant: binary counter vs arc counter counting circuits

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Binary counter uses standard binary positional encoding; arc counter uses rotation encoding with one qubit per binary digit, with higher-order qubits rotating at half the rate of the previous qubit.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Track the average distance traveled after n steps in a quantum walk/counting process.

problem_instance.description: Synthetic quantum-walk counting benchmark; no external financial dataset for this experiment. The paper compares average distance traveled after n steps for different counter designs.

dataset_specification.description: n steps from 0 to 10; 6-qubit counting register can represent 0 to 63

problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Ideal simulation, noisy simulation, and QPU results compared via average distance traveled; 1000 shots for deterministic circuits; QPU results reported in Table 2.

noise_model.noise_type: hardware noise and noisy simulation; exact noise model not specified

noise_parameters.estimated_compounded_gate_error_rate: ~40% for a 3-qubit circuit example discussed in motivation

speedup_claims.conditions: The paper emphasizes improved NISQ robustness rather than a computational speedup.
speedup_claims.caveats: No asymptotic or empirical speedup is claimed for this experiment.

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not established; the paper reports improved NISQ robustness for an 8-qubit arc counter and 6-qubit binary counter, but no asymptotic crossover analysis.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Would require larger, fault-tolerant circuits with lower two-qubit error rates; the paper emphasizes that binary counting is too gate-heavy and that the arc counter is easier to simulate classically.
limiting_factors: Arc counter is classically easy to simulate

notes: The paper explicitly reports a 6-qubit counting register for the simulations and an 11-qubit trapped-ion QPU for hardware runs.

Circuit depth and gate counts are not explicitly tabulated for this experiment; only qualitative statements about binary counter requiring many 2-qubit gates and arc counter using only single-qubit rotations are given.
No asymptotic speedup claim is made; the paper emphasizes improved NISQ robustness rather than speedup.
The paper explicitly says the arc counter has no physical quantum advantage because it is easy to model classically.
The binary counter becomes useless on noisy hardware, so there is no classical-vs-quantum advantage demonstrated.

experiments.description: Arc walk counter circuit combining a Hadamard coin with controlled rotation-based counting, evaluated in ideal simulation, noisy simulation, and on the trapped-ion QPU for 10-15 steps.

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Arc walk uses a Hadamard coin and controlled rotations on an 8-qubit counter register; higher-order qubits rotate at half the rate of the previous qubit.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Simulate a quantum walk / random walk position distribution with approximate counting.

problem_instance.description: Synthetic quantum walk benchmark with 8 counter qubits and 10-15 steps; compared in positive-only and two-way walk variants.

dataset_specification.description: 8-qubit register; 10 to 15 steps; 1000 shots per step

problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Average distance traveled and output distributions compared across ideal simulation, noisy simulation, and QPU.

noise_model.noise_type: hardware noise and noisy simulation; exact noise model not specified

speedup_claims.conditions: Simulation study of measurement frequency in a quantum walk.
speedup_claims.caveats: No classical baseline or speedup claim is reported.

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not established; the paper reports better robustness of the arc walk than the binary counter, but no classical baseline benchmark for the same task.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Would require scaling the approximate counting / quantum walk circuits beyond 8 qubits while preserving low two-qubit gate counts and noise tolerance.
limiting_factors: No classical baseline for the same distributional task
Noise and measurement effects dominate at current scale

notes: The paper explicitly states the arc walk results use an 8-qubit counter register and 1000 shots per job.
The QPU hardware is the same 11-qubit trapped-ion device referenced in the paper; the exact device name is not given in the excerpt.
No explicit circuit depth or gate counts are reported for this specific circuit.
The paper claims the arc walk is more reliable than binary counting on current hardware, but does not show a practical quantum advantage over classical methods.

experiments.description: Random jump circuit, with and without reversal/superposition post-processing, evaluated in ideal simulation using multiple randomly generated circuits per step.

algorithm.parameter_initialization: Randomly generated circuit instances per step; target qubit selected by weighted random sampling.

problem_formulation.encoding_details: A different target qubit is selected at each step according to a weighted random sampling distribution favoring lower-order qubits; optional reversal/superposition is done by classical post-processing.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Generate a random-walk-like distribution of positions with approximate counting and random jumps.

problem_instance.description: Synthetic random-walk benchmark with 8-qubit counter register; results shown for positive-only and two-way walk variants.

dataset_specification.description: Up to 9 steps; 30 random jump circuits per step; 30 shots per circuit

problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Averaged over 30 randomly generated circuits per step and 30 shots per circuit.

noise_model.noise_type: quantum randomness plus classical randomness in circuit generation; no hardware noise model specified

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Random circuit generation and weighted sampling of target qubits.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Optional reversal and superposition by subtracting down-circuit results from up-circuit results.

speedup_claims.conditions: Ideal simulation of randomly generated quantum walk circuits.
speedup_claims.caveats: No classical baseline or speedup claim is reported.

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not assessed; no hardware benchmark or classical baseline comparison is provided.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Would require hardware implementation and a classical comparison for the same random-walk distribution task.
limiting_factors: Classical randomness is also used in circuit generation

notes: The paper explicitly states an 8-qubit counter register and 30 shots per circuit, with 30 random circuits per step.
No hardware QPU is mentioned for this experiment; it is presented as an ideal simulation / generated-circuit study, so hardware.type is inferred as simulator_other.
No explicit circuit depth is reported.
The random jump circuit is evaluated only in ideal simulation and is explicitly described as easy to model classically.

experiments.description: Cascading disjunction circuit added to the random jump setup, evaluated in ideal simulation with and without reversal/superposition post-processing.

algorithm.variant: random jump circuit with cascading disjunctions
algorithm.parameter_initialization: Randomly generated circuits with randomly chosen lower- and higher-order bits for disjunction gates.

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Random jump circuit augmented with Boolean OR propagation between randomly chosen lower- and higher-order bits using Toffoli-based disjunction and ancilla reset.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Improve propagation of progress in the walk by allowing lower-order qubits to influence higher-order qubits.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Mid-circuit reset of ancilla qubit to enable reuse.

problem_instance.description: Synthetic random-walk benchmark with cascading disjunctions; positive-only and two-way walk variants shown.

dataset_specification.description: Up to 9 steps; 30 random jump circuits with cascading disjunctions per step; 30 shots per circuit

problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Averaged over 30 randomly generated circuits per step and 30 shots per circuit.

noise_model.noise_type: quantum randomness plus classical randomness in circuit generation; no hardware noise model specified

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Random circuit generation and weighted sampling of target qubits.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Optional reversal and superposition by subtracting down-circuit results from up-circuit results.

speedup_claims.conditions: Ideal simulation of random jump circuits with cascading disjunctions.
speedup_claims.caveats: No classical baseline or speedup claim is reported.

notes: The paper states the random jump circuit uses an 8-qubit counter register; cascading disjunction adds one ancilla qubit, so total qubits are inferred as 9.
No hardware QPU is mentioned for this experiment; it is an ideal simulation study.
No explicit circuit depth is reported.

experiments.description: Mid-circuit measurement study on the arc counter circuit, comparing walks with no mid-measurement, measurement every 7 steps, and measurement every step for 20-step walks.

algorithm.variant: arc counter circuit with mid-circuit measurement (quantum Zeno effect study)

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Arc counter circuit with periodic mid-circuit measurement and reset to study decoherence / Zeno-like suppression of motion.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Measure how mid-circuit measurement changes the average distance traveled in a quantum walk.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Mid-circuit measurement; reset implied where needed.

problem_instance.description: Synthetic 20-step quantum walk experiment comparing different mid-measurement frequencies.

dataset_specification.description: 20 steps; measurement every 7 steps vs every step vs none

problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Average positions reported for the three measurement schedules: 35.6, 14.3, and 5.7 respectively.

noise_model.noise_type: mid-circuit measurement / deliberate decoherence study in simulation

speedup_claims.conditions: Simulation study of mid-circuit measurement effects on a quantum walk.
speedup_claims.caveats: No classical baseline or speedup claim is reported.

notes: The paper reports the experiment as a simulation of 20-step walks with different measurement intervals, but does not specify the register size in the excerpted section.
No hardware QPU is mentioned; this is a simulation study.
No explicit circuit depth or shot count is given for this experiment.
